text: Space Exploration Technologies Corp., commonly known as SpaceX, is a private American aerospace and space transportation company headquartered at the Starbase development site in Starbase, Texas. Founded by Elon Musk in 2002, the company has advanced rocket propulsion, reusable launch vehicles, human spaceflight, and satellite constellation technology. As of 2025, SpaceX is the world's dominant space launch provider, with a launch cadence that surpasses all others, including private competitors and national programs like China's space program. SpaceX collaborates closely with NASA and the United States Armed Forces through governmental contracts. Musk founded SpaceX with the goal of reducing space launch costs to enable a self-sustaining colony on Mars. In 2008, the Falcon 1 successfully reached orbit after three prior failures. The company then developed the larger Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon 1 capsule to fulfill NASA's COTS contracts for resupply missions to the International Space Station. By 2012, SpaceX completed all COTS test flights and began Commercial Resupply Services missions. Around that time, the company began developing hardware to make the Falcon 9 first stage reusable, achieving the first successful first-stage landing in 2015 and re-launch in 2017. Falcon Heavy, built from three Falcon 9 boosters, made its first flight in 2018 after over a decade of development. As of May 2025, Falcon 9 rockets have landed and flown again more than 450 times, with launches occurring 1–3 times per week. These milestones brought significant investment, prompting SpaceX to diversify its income, with the Starlink satellite constellation launching its first operational satellite in 2019 and generating the bulk of the company's revenue, leading to the development of Starshield for military use. In 2020, SpaceX began operating Dragon 2 capsules for crewed missions to the International Space Station and private clients. The company also began building test prototypes for Starship, the largest launch vehicle in history, designed to be fully reusable, cost-effective, and adaptable. SpaceX is developing its own space suit and astronaut through the Polaris program and is building a human lander for NASA's Artemis lunar missions. SpaceX is not publicly traded but is expected to have an initial public offering in 2026. A space industry newspaper estimated SpaceX's revenue at over $10 billion in 2024, and a 2025 share buyout valued the company at $800 billion, making it the world's most valuable private company. In early 2001, Musk met Robert Zubrin and donated $100,000 to the Mars Society, joining its board briefly and giving a plenary talk where he announced Mars Oasis, a project to land a greenhouse on Mars. Musk attempted to acquire a Dnepr launch vehicle through Russian contacts from Jim Cantrell but found increasing resistance. On the flight home, Musk announced he would start a company to build affordable rockets. By applying vertical integration, using commercial off-the-shelf components when possible, and adopting software engineering principles, Musk believed SpaceX could significantly reduce launch costs. In early 2002, Musk began recruiting staff for the company, including Michael Griffin, Jim Cantrell, John Garvey, Tom Mueller, and Chris Thompson. SpaceX was initially headquartered in a warehouse in El Segundo, California, with early employees such as Tom Mueller, Gwynne Shotwell, and Chris Thompson coming from TRW and Boeing. By November 2005, the company had 160 employees, and Musk personally interviewed and approved all early hires. Musk stated one of his goals is to reduce the cost and improve the reliability of space access by a factor of ten. SpaceX developed the Falcon 1 with internal funding, a two-stage-to-orbit small-lift vehicle with a total development cost of approximately $90 million to $100 million. The Falcon rocket series is named after the Millennium Falcon from Star Wars. In 2004, SpaceX protested to the Government Accountability Office over a sole-source contract awarded to Kistler Aerospace, which NASA later withdrew and replaced with the COTS program. In 2005, SpaceX announced plans for a human-rated commercial space program that evolved into the Dragon spacecraft. In 2006, NASA awarded SpaceX $396 million for crew and cargo resupply demonstration missions under COTS. The first two Falcon 1 launches were purchased by the U.S. Department of Defense under the DARPA Falcon Project for hypersonic missile delivery. The first three Falcon 1 launches failed, nearly ending the company, and Tesla's financing also failed, leaving Musk, Tesla, and SolarCity nearly bankrupt; Musk reportedly experienced severe stress. The company turned around with the fourth Falcon 1 launch on September 28, 2008, after which Musk split his remaining $30 million between SpaceX and Tesla, and NASA awarded SpaceX a $1.6 billion Commercial Resupply Services contract in December, saving the company. The Falcon 1 was retired after its second successful and fifth total launch in July 2009, allowing focus on the Falcon 9. Gwynne Shotwell was promoted to company president for her role in securing the CRS contract. SpaceX originally planned to develop a Falcon 5 but instead chose to develop the Falcon 9, a reusable heavier lift vehicle, with development accelerated by NASA's commitment to purchase flights if capabilities were demonstrated, starting with $278 million from the COTS program. The first Falcon 9 launch with the Dragon Spacecraft Qualification Unit occurred in June 2010. The first operational Dragon spacecraft launched in December 2010 aboard COTS Demo Flight 1, safely returning to Earth after two orbits. By December 2010, the production line was manufacturing one Falcon 9 and Dragon every three months. In April 2011, NASA awarded SpaceX a $75 million contract to develop a launch escape system for Dragon, and in August 2012, a fixed-price Space Act Agreement was awarded to produce a detailed design of the crew transportation system. In early 2012, approximately two-thirds of SpaceX stock was owned by Musk, with his 70 million shares valued at $875 million on private markets, valuing the company at $1.3 billion. In May 2012, with the Dragon C2+ launch, Dragon became the first commercial spacecraft to deliver cargo to the International Space Station. After the flight, the private equity valuation nearly doubled to $2.4 billion or $20/share. By that time, SpaceX had raised approximately $1 billion over its first decade, with private equity contributing $200 million, Musk investing $100 million, and other investors contributing $100 million. SpaceX began its active reusability test program in late 2012 with low-altitude, low-speed landing tests, and high-velocity, high-altitude atmospheric return tests began in late 2013. In 2013, SpaceX launched its first commercial mission for a private customer. In 2014, the company won nine out of 20 globally competed contracts. Arianespace requested European government subsidies to counter SpaceX's competition. SpaceX's capabilities and pricing began affecting the U.S. military launch market, which had been dominated by United Launch Alliance for nearly a decade, with launch costs rising to over $400 million. In September 2014, NASA awarded SpaceX the Commercial Crew Transportation Capability (CCtCap) contract to finalize the development of the Crew Transportation System, including technical milestones, an uncrewed flight test, a crewed flight test, and six operational missions. In January 2015, SpaceX raised $1 billion from Google and Fidelity Investments, receiving 8.33% of the company and establishing a valuation of approximately $12 billion. The same month, SpaceX announced the development of the Starlink satellite constellation to provide global broadband internet with 4,000 satellites. In late June 2015, the seventh ISS resupply mission, CRS-7, exploded two minutes into flight due to a failed steel strut that caused a helium pressure vessel breach, leading to a high-pressure leak into a low-pressure propellant tank. SpaceX achieved the first successful landing and recovery of a first stage in December 2015 with Falcon 9 Flight 20. In April 2016, the company achieved the first successful landing on the autonomous spaceport drone ship Of Course I Still Love You in the Atlantic Ocean. By October 2016, SpaceX offered a 10% price discount to customers who flew on reused Falcon 9 first stages. In early September 2016, a Falcon 9 exploded during a propellant fill operation for a static fire test, destroying the $200 million AMOS-6 communications satellite. The explosion was caused by liquid oxygen solidifying and igniting with carbon composite helium vessels. The incident led to a four-month launch hiatus, with SpaceX returning to flight in January 2017. In March 2017, SpaceX launched a returned Falcon 9 for the SES-10 satellite, marking the first re-launch of a payload-carrying orbital rocket and the first landing of a reused orbital-class rocket. In July 2017, SpaceX raised $350 million, increasing its valuation to $21 billion. In 2017, SpaceX achieved a 45% global market share for commercial launch contracts. By March 2018, the company had over 100 launches on its manifest, representing about $12 billion in contract revenue, including both commercial and government customers, making it the leading global commercial launch provider by manifested launches. In 2017, SpaceX formed The Boring Company, which began constructing a short test tunnel adjacent to its headquarters, completed in May 2018 and opened to the public in December 2018. In 2018, The Boring Company was spun out as a separate entity with 6% of equity going to SpaceX, less than 10% to early employees, and the remainder to Elon Musk. In 2019, SpaceX raised $1.33 billion in capital across three funding rounds, with its valuation reaching $33.3 billion by May 2019 and $36 billion by March 2020. On August 19, 2020, after a $1.9 billion funding round, SpaceX's valuation increased to $46 billion. In February 2021, SpaceX raised an additional $1.61 billion from 99 investors at a per share value of approximately $420, raising the valuation to about $74 billion. By 2021, SpaceX had raised over $6 billion in equity financing, primarily used to support Starlink operations and Starship development. By October 2021, the valuation reached $100.3 billion. On April 16, 2021, Starship HLS won a contract to play a critical role in NASA's Artemis crewed spaceflight program. By 2021, SpaceX had agreements with Google Cloud Platform and Microsoft Azure to provide on-ground computer and networking services for Starlink. A 2022 funding round valued SpaceX at $127 billion. In July 2021, SpaceX unveiled a new drone ship, A Shortfall of Gravitas, which landed a booster from CRS-23 on August 29, 2021. Within the first 130 days of 2022, SpaceX conducted 18 rocket launches and two astronaut splashdowns. On December 13, 2021, CEO Elon Musk announced a carbon dioxide removal program to convert captured carbon into rocket fuel, following a $100 million donation to the X Prize Foundation in February 2021 to incentivize carbon capture technology development. In August 2022, Reuters reported that the European Space Agency began initial discussions with SpaceX to use its launchers temporarily due to Russia's blockade of Soyuz rockets during the invasion of Ukraine. Starlink was extensively used during the conflict. In 2022, the Falcon 9 became the world record holder for the most launches of a single vehicle type in a single year, launching approximately every six days with 61 total launches, all but one (a Falcon Heavy in November) being Falcon 9 launches. In November 2023, SpaceX announced it would acquire its parachute supplier Pioneer Aerospace out of bankruptcy for $2.2 million. On July 16, 2024, Elon Musk posted on X that SpaceX would move its headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to SpaceX Starbase in Brownsville, Texas, citing the recently passed California AB1955 bill.

In August 2022, Reuters reported that the European Space Agency (ESA) began initial discussions with SpaceX regarding the temporary use of its launchers, as Russia blocked access to Soyuz rockets during the invasion of Ukraine. Since the conflict, Starlink has been extensively used. In 2022, SpaceX's Falcon 9 became the world record holder for the most launches of a single vehicle type in a single year, with 61 launches total, approximately one every six days, all but one of which were on Falcon 9, including a Falcon Heavy launch in November. In November 2023, SpaceX acquired its parachute supplier Pioneer Aerospace out of bankruptcy for $2.2 million. On July 16, 2024, Elon Musk posted on X that SpaceX would move its headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to SpaceX Starbase in Brownsville, Texas, citing California AB1955, a law banning school districts from requiring teachers to notify parents about changes to a student's sexual orientation and gender identity, as a reason for the move. The headquarters officially relocated to Brownsville, Texas in August 2024, according to records filed with the California Secretary of State. The move was seen as largely symbolic in the short term, as the Hawthorne facility continued to support the company's Falcon launch vehicles, which remained SpaceX's workhorse product in 2024. SpaceX's 2024 Polaris Dawn mission featured the first-ever private spacewalk, a major milestone in commercial space exploration. In 2025, ProPublica reported that Chinese investors were investing in SpaceX via offshore entities such as the Cayman Islands, raising national security concerns, and later reported that Chinese equity ownership likely extended to direct investment, citing court testimony from investor Iqbaljit Kahlon. By July 2025, as part of a $5 billion equity raise, SpaceX agreed to invest $2 billion in xAI. In December 2025, Elon Musk confirmed the initial public offering (IPO) of SpaceX, scheduled for mid-2026, which analysts projected could be the largest IPO ever with a potential valuation over $1 trillion, despite CEO Musk having long rejected the idea of converting SpaceX into a publicly traded company. In January 2019, SpaceX announced a 10% workforce layoff to finance the Starship and Starlink projects. The Starship vehicle is designed to enable large-scale human and cargo transit to the Moon, Mars, and beyond, being the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown with a planned payload capacity of 100+ tons. Construction of initial prototypes and tests began in early 2019 in Florida and Texas, later moving to the new SpaceX South Texas launch site. On April 20, 2023, Starship's first orbital flight test ended in a mid-air explosion over the Gulf of Mexico before booster separation, with multiple engines failing and the vehicle reaching max q later than planned, eventually losing control and spinning until the automated flight termination system destroyed it; Elon Musk, SpaceX, and industry figures referred to the test as a success. Musk stated it would take "six to eight weeks" to prepare for the next launch, though a senior executive in October 2023 claimed the company had been ready since September, accusing regulators of disrupting progress and suggesting the delay could allow China to outpace U.S. astronauts in lunar missions. On November 18, 2023, SpaceX launched Starship on its second flight test, with both vehicles flying for a few minutes before exploding. In early March 2024, SpaceX targeted March 14 for its next uncrewed Starship launch, pending a FAA launch license, which was granted on March 13, 2024. On March 14, 2024, at 13:25 UTC, Starship launched for the first time on a planned suborbital trajectory, ending with the booster experiencing a malfunction shortly before landing and the ship being lost during re-entry over the Indian Ocean. On June 4, 2024, SpaceX received a launch license for its fourth flight test, notable for including a clause allowing subsequent test flights without a mishap investigation if the same launch profile and hardware specifications were met, potentially accelerating development. On October 12, 2024, SpaceX received FAA approval for its fifth flight test, the first without engine failures and the first successful tower catch. On November 19, 2024, SpaceX launched Starship on its sixth flight test, with the booster aborting the catch attempt and the ship conducting a relight in space. On January 16, 2025, SpaceX launched Starship on its seventh flight test, featuring the first Block 2 Ship, Ship 33 (403 ft or 123 meters), carrying a Starlink V3 simulator; the test resulted in the second catch of the Super Heavy booster, B14, but after eight minutes, contact was lost with the upper stage, leading to an explosion over the Atlantic Ocean near the Turks and Caicos Islands, prompting the FAA to require a mishap investigation. On March 7, 2025, SpaceX launched another Starship rocket from Texas, losing contact minutes into the flight and having the spacecraft come down and break apart, with wreckage seen across Florida's skies; preliminary investigation indicated an oxygen leak, flashes, and sustained fires in the aft section caused engine shutdown and activation of the self-destruct system. On June 18, 2025, a SpaceX Starship rocket exploded during a static fire test at the Starbase facility in Texas following a "major anomaly." A significant milestone occurred in May 2020 when SpaceX successfully launched two NASA astronauts, Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken, into orbit on a Crew Dragon spacecraft during Crew Dragon Demo-2, making SpaceX the first private company to send astronauts to the International Space Station and marking the first crewed orbital launch from American soil in nine years, launching from Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A in Florida. In May 2019, SpaceX launched the first large batch of 60 Starlink satellites, beginning deployment of what would become the world's largest commercial satellite constellation the following year. In 2022, most SpaceX launches focused on Starlink, a consumer internet business that sends batches of internet-beaming satellites and now has over 6,000 satellites in orbit. In July 2021, SpaceX entered an agreement to acquire Swarm Technologies, a private company building a low Earth orbit satellite constellation for IoT communications, for $524 million. In December 2022, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved the launch of up to 7,500 of SpaceX's next-generation satellites for its Starlink internet network. In September 2025, SpaceX announced it would purchase the rights to use some of EchoStar's spectrum for $17 billion in a cash and stock deal to use as a foundation for Starlink's direct-to-cell business globally. SpaceX has developed three launch vehicles: the small-lift Falcon 1, retired in 2009 after five launches with two successes, making it the first privately funded, liquid-fueled rocket to reach orbit; the medium-lift Falcon 9, capable of delivering up to 22,800 kilograms to orbit, with nine Merlin engines in its first stage, first reaching orbit on June 4, 2010, and successfully launching the first commercial spacecraft to dock with the ISS on May 22, 2012, upgraded to v1.1 in 2013, Full Thrust in 2015, and Block 5 in 2018, with its first stage designed to land, be recovered, and fly again; and the heavy-lift Falcon Heavy, capable of delivering up to 63,800 kg to LEO or 26,700 kg to GTO, using three modified Falcon 9 first-stage cores with 27 Merlin 1D engines, which successfully flew its inaugural mission on February 6, 2018, launching Musk's personal Tesla Roadster into heliocentric orbit. Both Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy are certified for National Security Space Launch (NSSL) missions, with 601 launches as of January 18, 2026, resulting in 598 full mission successes, one partial success, and one in-flight failure, plus a pre-flight failure in 2016. As of 2017, the Starship system was intended to supersede existing launch vehicles by the early 2020s. SpaceX has developed several rocket engines—Merlin, Kestrel, and Raptor—for launch vehicles, Draco for the reaction control system of the Dragon spacecraft, and SuperDraco for crew abort capability in Crew Dragon. Merlin uses liquid oxygen and RP-1, powering the Falcon 1 first stage and both stages of Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy; Kestrel uses the same propellants and powered the Falcon 1 second stage. Draco and SuperDraco are hypergolic liquid-propellant engines; Draco is used on the Dragon and Dragon 2 reaction control systems, while eight SuperDraco engines provide launch escape capability for Crew Dragon 2. Raptor is a liquid oxygen and liquid methane-fueled full-flow staged combustion engine for Starship, with development versions test-fired in late 2016 and first flight in 2019, powering the Starhopper to 20 meters. SpaceX has developed the Dragon spacecraft for cargo and crew transport to the International Space Station. The first-generation Dragon 1 was used only for cargo, developed under NASA's COTS program, with a successful demonstration flight in 2010 and a CRS contract awarded. The second-generation Dragon 2 conducted its first uncrewed flight to the ISS in early 2019, followed by a crewed flight in 2020, developed under NASA's Commercial Crew Program; the cargo variant flew for the first time in December 2020. In March 2020, SpaceX revealed Dragon XL, designed as a resupply spacecraft for NASA's Lunar Gateway under a GLS contract, capable of transporting over 5,000 kg to the Gateway and docked for six to twelve months. SpaceX designed a spacesuit for use inside the Dragon spacecraft to protect against depressurization and unveiled a second spacesuit in May 2024 for extravehicular activity, planned for use during the Polaris Dawn mission. SpaceX routinely returns the first stage of Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets after orbital launches, landing at a predetermined site using only its propulsion systems or returning to an autonomous spaceport drone ship in the ocean if propellant margins do not allow a return to launch site. SpaceX had plans to introduce floating launch platforms, modified oil rigs, as a sea launch option for Starship; as of February 2023, the company had sold the oil rigs but had not ruled out future sea-based platforms. Starlink is an internet satellite constellation under development by Starlink Services, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of SpaceX, consisting of thousands of cross-linked communications satellites in ~550 km orbits, aiming to meet global demand for low-cost broadband. Development began in 2015, with prototype test-flights launched in 2017 on the Paz mission; the first batch of 60 satellites was launched in May 2019 on a Falcon 9. Initial test operations began in late 2020 and first orders were taken in early 2021, with customers expecting internet speeds of 50 Mbit/s to 150 Mbit/s and latency from 20 ms to 40 ms. In December 2022, Starlink reached over 1 million subscribers worldwide. The large number of satellites has been criticized by astronomers for light pollution in both optical and radio wavelengths, interfering with scientific observations, prompting SpaceX to implement upgrades to reduce brightness. The large number also creates long-term space debris collision risks, though satellites are equipped with krypton-fueled Hall thrusters to de-orbit at end-of-life and are designed to autonomously avoid collisions based on uplinked tracking data. In December 2022, SpaceX announced Starshield, a program to incorporate military or government payloads on Starlink-derived satellites, with the Space Development Agency as a key customer for a space-based missile defense system. In June 2024, SpaceX introduced a compact version of its Starlink antennas, the "Starlink Mini," designed for mobile satellite internet use, offered for $599 in an early access release, more expensive than the base model.
